title: Dorando: Won and Lost in the Marathon
subtitle: In 1908 a small Italian runner came into the Olympic stadium in first place. Then something went wrong — and the world never forgot it.
footer: Story Lesson · Past Simple and Past Continuous · A2/B1
intention: you'll follow a true race story and tell your own stories with the past simple and past continuous, so you can say what happened and what was happening around it.
warmup: Have you ever done something long and difficult? What was it? Did you want to stop?
Why do some people run long races? What do they enjoy about it?
Think of a sport event you remember. Where were you? What happened?

vocab.heading: A · What do they mean? Guess from the sentence
vocab.intro: Read the sentence and guess the word in bold. Say your idea out loud. Then reveal.

items.sent: A good runner doesn't start too fast. She runs at a steady pace.
items.meaning: pace (noun) — how fast you run: a slow pace, a fast pace.

items.sent: After thirty kilometres he was very tired. His legs felt empty. He had no more energy, and every step was hard.
items.meaning: energy (noun) — the power in your body to do things, like running or working.

items.sent: There were more than fifty runners in the race, and they all wanted to win.
items.meaning: runner (noun) — a person who runs, especially in a race.

items.sent: She ran 21 kilometres in under two hours. It was her personal best — her fastest time ever.
items.meaning: personal best (noun) — your own best result so far.

vocab.heading: B · More words from the race
vocab.intro: Same idea: guess from the sentence, then reveal.

items.sent: On the last bend he passed two runners and moved into third place.
items.meaning: pass (verb) — to go past someone who is moving in the same direction.

items.sent: After thirty kilometres she was in the lead. Nobody was in front of her.
items.meaning: in the lead (phrase) — in first place; in front of everyone.

items.sent: He was so tired that he staggered across the grass, with his arms out for balance.
items.meaning: stagger (verb) — to walk in an unsteady way because you are very tired.

vocab.heading: C · After the race
vocab.intro: These three words are important in the story. Guess, then reveal.

items.sent: The runner collapsed suddenly on the road. The doctors ran to help him.
items.meaning: collapse (verb) — to fall down suddenly because you are very tired, weak or ill.

items.sent: The judges said: “You broke the rules, so you cannot win.” They disqualified the team.
items.meaning: disqualify (verb) — to officially take someone out of a competition because they broke the rules.

items.sent: The coach was angry. He made a protest and asked the judges to change the result.
items.meaning: protest (noun) — a formal complaint to the judges of a competition.

What job or hobby needs a lot of energy? Why?
Have you ever thought a result was not fair? What happened?
story_heading: Dorando Pietri and the 1908 Olympic Marathon

story.heading: Part 1 — A hot afternoon
paras: On 24 July 1908, the Olympic Games were in London. The marathon was starting. The race began at Windsor Castle and finished in a new stadium. The route was about 42 kilometres — 26 miles and 385 yards. After this race, people used the same distance for every marathon.

More than fifty runners started the race. It was a very hot day. Many runners went too fast at the beginning. Later they were tired and slow. Some stopped at the side of the road, and ambulances took them away.

One runner was Dorando Pietri. He was twenty-two and from a small town in Italy called Carpi. He worked in a sweet shop. He was small and not famous. He did not run at the front. He ran at a steady pace. While the other runners were getting tired, he was moving past them, one by one.
checks: Where did the race start and finish?
What happened to many runners? Why?
How did Dorando run? What was he doing while the others were getting tired?
answers: It started at Windsor Castle and finished in a stadium in London.
Many went too fast at the beginning, so they became tired and slow in the heat. Some stopped.
He ran at a steady pace. He was passing the other runners one by one.
story.discuss: What is better in a long race — a fast start or a slow, steady start? What about in other things, like study or work?

story.heading: Part 2 — The stadium
paras: Dorando came into the stadium in the lead, in first place. About 75,000 people were waiting, and they were shouting and cheering. But Dorando looked terrible. He had no energy left.

Then he turned the wrong way. Some officials ran to him and showed him the right way. A few steps later, his legs stopped working and he collapsed. He got up and staggered forward a little more. Then he fell again. Most people say he fell five times in the last part of the race.

The doctors and officials ran to him. The crowd was shouting. Someone took his arm and helped him stand. With people on both sides, Dorando walked slowly to the finishing line. He crossed it in 2 hours 54 minutes. The stadium was roaring.
checks: Where was Dorando when he came into the stadium?
What mistake did he make? What did the officials do?
How did he cross the finishing line?
answers: He was in first place, and 75,000 people were cheering.
He turned the wrong way. The officials showed him the right way.
People helped him. They held him on both sides and he walked slowly to the line.
story.discuss: You are standing next to Dorando. Do you help him? Why or why not?

story.heading: Part 3 — The decision
paras: The crowd thought Dorando was the winner. But very soon the American team made a protest. Their runner, Johnny Hayes, came in just after Dorando. The Americans said: “People helped Dorando. That is against the rules.”
The judges agreed. They disqualified Dorando, and Johnny Hayes got the gold medal.

But that was not the end of the story. Everyone in London talked about Dorando. The newspapers wrote about him, and the famous writer Arthur Conan Doyle described the race. The next day, Queen Alexandra gave Dorando a special silver cup. Someone wrote a song about him. Later, he ran in exhibition races in other countries.
The rule was clear, and Hayes kept his gold medal. But today, more than a hundred years later, many people remember Dorando, not Hayes.
checks: Why did the American team protest?
What happened to Dorando after the race?
answers: They said people helped Dorando to finish, and this was against the rules.
They disqualified Dorando. Johnny Hayes got the gold medal.
He became famous. The Queen gave him a silver cup, people wrote about him and a song was written about him.
story.discuss: The judges followed the rules, but people remember Dorando. Why do you think that happened?

grammar.name: Past Simple and Past Continuous
grammar.lead: To tell a good story you need two kinds of past: what happened (the events) and what was happening (the scene around the events). Look at the story.
notes: 1 · Past simple — the events, one after another. “Dorando came into the stadium. He turned the wrong way. He fell.” Each verb is a new step in the story.
2 · Past continuous — the scene, what was happening. Form: was / were + verb-ing. “75,000 people were cheering.” “The crowd was shouting.”
3 · Together. A long action (past continuous) and a short event (past simple): “While the leaders were getting tired, Dorando passed them.” “Someone took his arm while he was lying on the track.”
4 · Time words. while + past continuous (the long action). when + past simple (the short event): “When he entered the stadium, the people were cheering.”

5 · Be careful. We do not use the past continuous for a finished series of events. He was falling five times. → “He fell five times.” And verbs like know and want are usually past simple: “He wanted to finish.”

exercises.heading: Past simple or past continuous?
exercises.intro: Put the verb in brackets in the correct form. Read the whole sentence first.
items: 1. The sun ___ (shine) and it was very hot when the race started.
2. Dorando ___ (come) into the stadium, and the people ___ (cheer).
3. While the doctors ___ (help) him, the crowd ___ (shout).
4. He ___ (fall) five times before he reached the line.
5. When the Americans ___ (protest), the judges ___ (listen) carefully.
answers: 1. was shining (a scene, in the background)
2. came / were cheering (an event, then the scene)
3. were helping / was shouting (two actions going on at the same time)
4. fell (a finished series of events)
5. protested / listened (one event, then the next event)

exercises.heading: Find the mistake
exercises.intro: Each sentence has one mistake with the verb. Write the sentence correctly.
items: 1. While the leaders got tired, Dorando passed them.
2. The judges were deciding that he broke the rules.
3. Dorando was lying on the track when someone was taking his arm.
4. The crowd shouted when Dorando was entering the stadium.
5. The Queen was giving him a silver cup the next day.
answers: 1. While the leaders were getting tired, Dorando passed them.
2. The judges decided that he broke the rules.
3. Dorando was lying on the track when someone took his arm.
4. The crowd was shouting when Dorando entered the stadium.
5. The Queen gave him a silver cup the next day.

exercises.heading: Tell the story
exercises.intro: Write one sentence for each note. Use the past simple or the past continuous. Then say the whole story aloud.
items: 5. (event + scene) the Americans / protest / while / the crowd / still / cheer → ___
answers: 1. The day was very hot. (or: It was a very hot day.)
2. Dorando came into the stadium.
3. 75,000 people were cheering.
4. He turned the wrong way.
5. The Americans protested while the crowd was still cheering.

grammar.closing: Now tell the Dorando story out loud in about one minute. Use the past simple for events and the past continuous for the scene.

deeper.heading: Going deeper — the rule, the numbers and the language
deeper.lead: This story is not only about one runner. It asks a question about fairness. It also explains the distance of the races people run today.

blocks.heading: Where do 42 km and 21 km come from?
paras: After the 1908 Games, the marathon distance became 42.195 kilometres — about the same as the route from Windsor Castle to the stadium. A half marathon is half of this: 21.0975 kilometres, or 13.1 miles.
Today the half marathon is one of the most popular races in the world. Many ordinary people train for a few months and run it.

items.q: How long is a half marathon in kilometres?
Which race made the marathon distance famous?
Say it in the past simple: “Dorando falls.”

blocks.heading: Was it fair?
paras: People still talk about the decision. Both sides have a good reason.

pairs.b: The rule was clear: no help. Johnny Hayes ran the whole race alone. If helped runners can win, the race is not fair.
He was first to the line. The officials wanted to protect him. He did not ask for help, so it is not fair to punish him.

blocks.heading: Talking about a race
paras: These phrases are useful for any race. Complete each sentence, then reveal.

items.q: We set ___ at nine o'clock. (the word that means “started the journey”)
I ___ a personal best today. (made / set)
The last kilometre was very hard. I was ___ (hang on) to the end.
items.a: hanging on — meaning “I was only just able to continue”.

discuss: Is finishing a race more important than winning it?
Should a rule always be used, even when the result feels unfair?
Why do people often cheer more for the runner who is struggling than for the winner?

speak.intro: Now it's your turn. Choose a task, start the timer and talk. Try to use both the past simple and the past continuous.
speak.useful: “It was … when …” · “While I was …, … happened” · “First, … Then, … After that, …” · “I felt …” · “The best moment was when …”

tasks.label: Task 1 — I wanted to stop
paras: Tell me about a time you wanted to stop but kept going. What was happening? What did you do?

tasks.label: Task 2 — The event
paras: Tell the story of a race, a match, a trip or another event you took part in. What happened first? Next? Last?

tasks.label: Task 3 — Getting ready
paras: Tell me about something you practised for weeks or months. What did you do? Did it go well?

tasks.label: Task 4 — The decision
paras: Was it fair to disqualify Dorando? Give your opinion for two minutes. Then argue the other side.

final: People remember Dorando more than the winner. Why do you think this happens?
The Americans followed the rules. Were they right to make a protest?
Is it better to be a famous loser or an unknown winner?
From memory: tell the Dorando story in five sentences. Use the past simple and the past continuous.
